peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Editor’s and Reviewers’ Comment
We thank the editor and reviewers for their suggestions and constructive comments.
The offered comments were taken carefully and we have responded to the queries and
comments raised by the referees and accordingly revised the manuscript. As per the
reviewer’s suggestions, the carried-out amendments and revisions are differentiated
by using red color font in the revised manuscript.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In the manuscript “Thermal tolerance and cellular plasticity in marine phytoplankton
diatoms modulated by epigenetic mechanisms for environmental adaptation” authors
investigated the role of the heat shock transcription factor 2 (HSF2) in the thermal
tolerance in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum and uncovered PtCdc45-like gene
as one of the major targets of PtHSF2. The work explores a little understood
mechanism in thermo tolerance of an important group of phytoplankton.
I am fully aware that functional studies in diatoms are not easy to carry out and I
appreciate the use of state-of-the-art techniques such as CUT&Tag. However, I am
convinced that several open questions need to be addressed (in a way that is feasible
to do in diatoms) to draw conclusions about the mechanism of HSF2 action.
Response: We appreciate the time and effort that you have dedicated to providing
your valuable feedback on our manuscript.The provided comments are considered
carefully and carried out the experiments.
Major comments:
1. The most important issue is for me the missing analysis of the impact of HSF2 and
Cdc45-like gene on the cell cycle progression. First of all, the authors report that both
HSF2 and Cdc45-like over-expressing strains have wider cells than the respective
control strains, resulting in higher cell volume. Authors themselves speculate that this
could be due to a cell cycle arrest (line 312). The presence of two chloroplasts per cell
in Figure 1F for PtHSF2 over-expression strains and Figure 3B for PtCdc45-like over-
expression strains further supports the idea of cell accumulation/cell cycle arrest in the
S or G2 phase, which could explain the higher cell volume. Moreover, the Cdc45
protein is a conserved member of eukaryotic replisomes. Therefore, the analysis of the
cell cycle progression of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like is essential to understand the
phenotypes induced by over-expression and knock-down of these genes.
Verifying the presence or absence of cell cycle arrest is important also for the
interpretation of the RNAseq results, as it was shown that many genes in diatoms
show cell cycle stage-dependent expression.
Response:Thank you for your insightful and detailed comments. We agree that
analyzing the impact of HSF2 and Cdc45-like genes on cell cycle progression is
crucial to understanding the observed phenotypes. We haveaddressed your concerns
as follows:
(1)Analysis of Cell Cycle Progression: As you mentioned, both HSF2 and
Cdc45-like over-expressing strains exhibit wider cells and higher cell volume, which
we speculated might be due to cell cycle arrest.Research has indicated that
chloroplast division in Phaeodactylum tricornutum occurs during the S phase 1. We
synchronized exponentially growing cells by subjecting them to an extended dark
period (20 h) and then transferred them to fresh medium for normal culture (12 h light:
12 h dark). Samples were collected at consistent culture times for confocal analysis,
revealing that the enlarged cells contained two chloroplasts.This finding further
supports the idea of cell accumulation or cell cycle arrest in the S or G2 phase. (L. No.
537-544, 773-775, 793, 1291-1293, Fig. 1D and Fig. 3E)
(2) Flow Cytometry Analysis: To address this issue, we have performed flow
cytometry analysis to examine the DNA content and determine the cell cycle
distribution of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like transgenic strains. It was found that PtHSF2
and PtCdc45-like overexpression cells exhibited cell accumulation or cell cycle arrest
in the S or G2 phase. (L. No. 375-387, 543-544, 983-995, Supplementary Fig. 8)
(3) RNAseq Data Reanalysis:We recognize that cell cycle arrest could influence
gene expression profiles. Therefore, verifying the cell cycle status of our strains is
essential for accurately interpreting the RNAseq data. Given the cell cycle-dependent
expression of many genes in diatoms, we reanalyzed the RNA sequencing results and
identified several cell cycle-related genes that were significantly differentially
expressed. (L. No. 387-390, Supplementary Table 6)
We have included the results of these additional experiments and analyses in the
revised manuscript to provide a comprehensive understanding of the impact of HSF2
and Cdc45-like genes on cell cycle progression and the associated phenotypes.
2. To further test the hypothesis that PtCdc45-like is a direct target of PtHSF2 and part
of PtHSF2 overexpression phenotype is mediated by PtCdc45 overexpression, I
suggest testing whether PtCdc45-like downregulation can alleviate part of the PtHSF2
overexpression phenotype. The authors have all the constructs/strains to test this
genetic interaction.
Response:Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We agree that investigating the
phenotypic differences between PtCdc45-like RNAi lines and PtHSF2 overexpressing
lines could further elucidate the phenotypic changes caused by the upregulation of
PtCdc45-like expression in PtHSF2 overexpressing strains. This will provide crucial
insights into the genetic interaction between PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like.
We have knocked down PtCdc45-like in the PtHSF2 overexpression backgroundto
observe phenotypic changes.These experiments included measuring cell size and
monitoring cell density to determine if the PtHSF2-induced phenotypes are mediated
by PtCdc45-like.These results have been included in our revised manuscript. (L. No.
401-405, 420-424, 710-718, 1372-1373, Supplementary Fig. 9A-C, Fig. 4E and F)
I recommend to address the above questions and adjust the discussion and conclusions
according to the results that will be obtained.
Response:Thank you again for your constructive comments on our manuscript, and
we have revised the discussion and conclusions.
Minor comments:
3. Title of the article - I find the title very general. It’s perhaps only my personal
preference, but I recommend using a title that better describes the findings of the
presented research, including the names of the studied genes.
Response:Thank you for your valuable feedback. We agree that the title could be
more specific to better reflect the findings of our research. We have revised the title to
more accurately describe the studied genes and their roles in thermal tolerance and
cellular plasticity. (L. No. 2-4)
4. Methods explaining how were obtained results presented in Supplementary Figure
1 are missing.
Response: We apologize for omitting this part of the methodand appreciate your
meticulous scrutiny.We have added the methods for obtaining the results shown in
Supplementary Figure 1 in the Methods section. (L. No. 643-657, 663-674)
5. Supplementary Figure 1 C shows that the abundance of PtHSF2 homologs is
highest at higher latitudes and relatively low in tropical parts of the oceans. How can
it be explained?
Response: Supplementary Fig. 1 Cpresents the geographic distribution and
abundance of PtHSF2 homologous genes, and in combination with Supplementary
Fig. 1 B we find that these homologous genes are mainly derived from diatoms
(Bacillariophyta). These results suggested that diatoms were particularly abundant at
high latitudes, which were consistent with previous reports 2, 3.In terms of why
diatoms are more abundant at higher latitudes, there are mainly the following reasons:
(i) the availability of nutrients such as nitrate, phosphate and silicate is higher at
higher latitudes 4 (ii) although diatoms have extensive temperature tolerance,most
diatoms grow better in cooler water 5, 6. (L. No. 149-153)
6. Please give a better explanation for Supplementary Figure 1B.
Response: We apologize for the lack of a detailed explanation of this part of the
results, which led to an inconvenience in understanding.We have provided a detailed
explanation in the manuscript. (L. No. 143-147)
7. Taking into account the focus of this study on heat stress tolerance, I am missing
information about the expression of the expression of the PtHSF2 gene at 20C and
30C.
Response: Thank you for your valuable feedback. We acknowledge the importance of
including data on PtHSF2 gene expression at different temperatures, given the focus
of this study on heat stress tolerance. Through qPCR analysis, we observed a
significant increase in PtHSF2 expression at 30 °C compared to its expression level at
20 °C in the wild-type background. (L. No. 138-142, 627-629, 1437-1440, Fig. 1A)
8. Authors show that they generated PtHSF2 RNAi lines, but there is no analysis done
with these lines. If there is no phenotypic difference from wild-type, it is necessary to
mention it at least in the text. Also, the thermotolerance of PtCdc45-like RNAi lines
should be shown.
Response: Thank you for your professional comments, we agree with this. We have
analyzed the characterization of PtHSF2 RNAi lines and added the results to the text
(L. No. 180-181, 192-194, 211-212, Fig.1C-H). We have also tested and
supplemented the thermotolerance of PtCdc45-like RNAi lines. (L. No. 455-456, Fig.
5)
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript by Huang et al. reveals the role of epigenetic mechanisms in
facilitating the adaptation of marine phytoplankton to environmental stress, with a
focus on the thermal tolerance and cellular plasticity. The insights gleaned are
pivotal in understanding and projecting marine ecosystem responses to global warming.
Notably, it marks the application of a novel CUT&Tag technique to decode the
operational mechanism of transcription factor PtHSF2 within microalgae. Overall,
this manuscript appears to be well-positioned for acceptance, given its novelty and
relevance to a broad readership interested in marine biology, climate change, and
epigenetics. However, I have several other comments on this manuscript, and they
should be considered before the paper can be published.
Response: We thank you for reviewing our manuscript and giving us the opportunity
to revise it.The provided comments and concerns were considered carefully, and we
have modified the manuscript as per the suggestions.
Major points:
1. The authors mention in the manuscript that P. tricornutum has 69 heat shock
transcription factors (HSFs), but have not explained why PtHSF2 was chosen for this
study. The authors should explain it.
Response:We appreciate your insightful comment. Our decision to focus on PtHSF2
was driven by preliminary analyses of relative transcript levels, which indicated that
its expression levels showed significant variation with temperature changes. This
observation suggested that PtHSF2 might play a crucial role in the temperature
response mechanism of P. tricornutum.We have incorporated this important result
into the revised manuscript as Fig. 1A and made corresponding modifications to the
content of the manuscript. (L. No. 138-142, Fig. 1A)
2. CUT&Tag technology is a highly sensitive and streamlined method for studying
protein-DNA interactions on chromatin, offering advantages such as low background
noise and suitability for single-cell analysis. However, there is few report of its
application in algae. To promote the application of this technology in the field of algal
research, I suggest specifying the relevant experimental details, such as
electroporation parameters, including voltage and pulse duration in Line 525.
Response: We are grateful for this suggestion. We have added a detailed description
according to the comment. (L. No. 894-895)
Minor points:

Response: Thank you for pointing this out.This phrase was modified according to the

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Report on the manuscript NCOMMS-24-06983
The manuscript “Thermal tolerance and cellular plasticity in marine phytoplankton
diatoms modulated by epigenetic mechanisms for environmental adaptation” by
Huang et al relates to the molecular mechanisms involved in the acclimatory response
of diatom to increased sea water temperature condition. Available evidences indicate
that diatoms, a prominent group of marine primary producers, present a larger thermal
tolerance range than other phytoplankton functional types. Knowledge on the
mechanisms involved in diatom thermal tolerance range, however, are limited. Huang
et al report an expansion of the transcription factor Heat Shock Factors (HSFs) in
diatom genomes. In addition, reverse genetic approach carried out in the model
diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum suggests that the HSF orthologue HSF2 may play
a positive role in the response to increased temperature via transcriptional activation
of the target cyclin dependent kinase Cdc45-like with concurrent effects on cell size
and growth, lipid and oxidative stress metabolisms.
Documentation on the molecular mechanisms involved in the thermal tolerance of
marine microalgae is central to better understand their ecophysiology and predict their
response to ongoing ocean warming. This topic, therefore, is of particular interest for
a large and broad audience. The introduction is concise and focused, presenting well
the background and needed research. The result section follows a logical sequence
and the choice of the methods and approaches are sound and complementary.
However, while the manuscript presents valuable novel information their significance
remains relatively limited.Specifically, while the manuscript suggests that HSF2 and
Cdc45-like may play a positive role in the tolerance of P. tricornutum to increased
temperature it remains to be addressed if this mechanism is conserved in diatoms eg
by providing evidences on the role of HSF2 in different diatom species of contrasting
thermal tolerance ranges and/or in another model diatom species of contrasting
ecophysiology such as Thalassiosira pseudonana. In addition, it remains unknown
whether HSF2 and Cdc45-like directly contribute to the apparent larger thermal
tolerance range observed in diatoms compared to that in other phytoplankton
functional types eg are HSF2 and Cdc45-like orthologues absent or regulated
differently in coccolithophores and green algae? Also, the experimental approach
focuses on the response to increased temperature but does not address the acclimatory
response to decreased temperature thus limiting our understanding on the importance
of HSF2 and Cdc45-like for the diatom thermal tolerance range per se. In addition,
and importantly, I think that in some instances the designs of the experiments have
shortcomings, the experiments are incomplete and the data are not presented in a clear
way - altogether this reduces the solidity of the results and conclusions. In
consequence I believe that the manuscript in its current version is not suited for
publication in Nature Communications. This is a very interesting topic and the work
carried out by Huang et al is substantial. I have provided below my detailed
comments and suggestions, which I hope, may contribute to improve the manuscript.
Response: Thank you for your thorough review and insightful comments on our
manuscript. We greatly appreciate your feedback and constructive suggestions, which
have helped us enhance the quality and robustness of our study.Below, we have
addressed each of your concerns in detail:
(1) Conservation of the Mechanism in Other Diatom Species: We understand the
importance of exploring whether the mechanisms we identified are conserved across
different diatom species, especially those with varying thermal tolerance ranges. In
our study, we conducted high-temperature treatments on Thalassiosira weissflogii at
30°C and 35°C, followed by transcriptome sequencing analysis. The results showed
that, compared to 20°C, the expression levels of the HSF2 orthologue (snap_masked-
ctg119-processed-gene-4.14-mRNA-1, 48.5% similarity) in Thalassiosira weissflogii
significantly increased with rising temperatures, showing 1.21-fold and 1.92-fold
upregulation at 30°C and 35°C, respectively. As shown in the Supplementary Table 13,
the Cdc45-like orthologue (snap_masked-ctg1929-processed-gene-0.66-mRNA-1,
53.4% similarity) also exhibited an upregulation trend. Based on these findings, we
hypothesize that the HSF2 transcription factor is a key regulator of heat tolerance in
diatoms, and this regulatory role may be widespread among diatoms.
(2)Comparison with Other Phytoplankton Functional Types: Furthermore, to
investigate whether HSF2 and Cdc45-like contribute to the broader temperature
tolerance range observed in diatoms compared to other phytoplanktons, We conducted
orthologue comparison analyses across the genomes of several sequenced microalgae,
including Emiliania huxleyi (a coccolithophore) and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (a
green alga). The results showed that the HSF2 orthologue (XP_005770267.1) was
present in E. huxleyi with a sequence similarity of 39.7%, while no orthologue for
Cdc45-like was detected. In C. reinhardtii, both HSF2 orthologue (XP_001702071.2)
and Cdc45-like orthologue (XP_001696501.1) were identified, with sequence
similarities of 37.9% and 26.3%, respectively (Supplementary Table 13). These
findings indicate that the HSF2 orthologs and Cdc45-like genes in E. huxleyi and C.
reinhardtii exhibit lower similarity, or even absence, compared to their diatom
counterparts. These results suggest that these microalgae might rely on distinct
genetic mechanisms to regulate their response to temperature fluctuations. Given
these findings, the absence or low similarity of HSF2 and Cdc45-like orthologs in
coccolithophores and green algae might contribute to their narrower thermal tolerance
range compared to diatoms. Together, these analyses imply that HSF2 and Cdc45-like
genes might play a more central role in the thermal tolerance mechanisms of diatoms,
potentially explaining their broader adaptability to temperature fluctuations.These
updates have been reflected in the revised manuscript. (L. No. 460-469, 543-555)
(3)Acclimatory Response to Decreased Temperature: We acknowledge that our
initial manuscript exclusively focused on investigating the response to elevated
temperatures.We have conducted additional experiments to assess the role of HSF2
and Cdc45-like in the acclimatory response to decreased temperature (15 ℃).The
results indicated that overexpressing cells did not demonstrate a growth advantage at
low temperatures (15 ℃), and no significant differences were observed between the
RNAi strains and the wild-type (Fig. 1C and Fig. 3C).This provides a more
comprehensive understanding of their roles in the thermal tolerance range of diatoms.
We have added these results to the revised manuscript. (L. No. 179-184, 327-330)
(4)Experimental Design and Data Presentation: We appreciate your feedback
regarding the experimental design and data presentation.To improve the reliability of
our results and conclusions, we have made every effort to address the shortcomings in
the experimental design and the areas where the experiments were incomplete.

Response to Editor and Reviewers
We would like to thank the editor and reviewers for their time and valuable feedback,
which have been very helpful in improving the clarity and quality of our manuscript.
Below, we provide detailed responses to each comment and indicate the changes made
in the manuscript.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Overall, this manuscript is much improved following the authors’ response to the
comments from all reviewers. The additional experiments helped to clarify the
relationships between the investigated genes (PtHSF2 and PtCDC45) and their
influence on the thermal tolerance in the diatom Phaedactylum tricornutum. I have no
major comments but just two minor comments below.
Line 138- 140 — I am still missing a better explanation of why you focused solely on
the PtHSF2. It is mentioned that this the transcripts of this HSF varies significantly with
the temperature. But is this different from the other HSFs? Could you show the
underlying data for other HSF to illustrate better your choice of HSF2?
Response: Thank you for your valuable feedback. Based on RNA-seq and differential
gene expression analysis from our preliminary experiments, we found that PtHSF2
(Phatr3_J55070) is the most significantly upregulated HSF under elevated temperature
conditions (Supplementary Table 3). Specifically, P. tricornutum was cultured at 20°C
and 30°C for 7 days, followed by RNA-seq analysis. Differential expression analysis
was conducted using the criteria of |log₂(fold change)| > 1 to identify significantly
differentially expressed genes. The results revealed a significant upregulation of
PtHSF2 expression with the temperature shift from 20°C to 30°C, making it the top-
upregulated HSF among all detected heat shock factors. Based on these findings, we
hypothesize that PtHSF2 plays a key role in the heat stress response, which led us to
focus on its functional characterization in this manuscript. (L. No. 135-137)
Line 278-282 - I recommend calling the identified sequence “putative consensus motif”.
Confirmation that it is the main target sequence of HSF2 binding needs additional
experiments.
Response:Thank you for your insightful suggestion. We agree with your viewpoint and
hand
have revised the manuscript to describe the sequence as a “putative consensus motif,”
appropriately reflecting the preliminary nature of our findings. (L. No. 262)
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
My concerns have been addressed in the revisions.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your positive feedback and are delighted that our
revisions have effectively addressed your concerns.

The manuscript has been substantially improved. Here are some minor comments.
1. The author address needs to be checked.
Response: Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We have thoroughly reviewed
and revised the author address to ensure its consistency and accuracy across the
manuscript. (L. No. 16)
2. Line 139, how about the transcriptional expression of other HSFs? Average value
significantly lower than HSF2?
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. In our preliminary experiments, P.
tricornutum was cultured at 20°C and 30°C for 7 days,followed by RNA-seq analysis.
Using a threshold of |log₂(fold change)| > 1 to identify significantly differentially
expressed genes, we found that PtHSF2 (Phatr3_J55070) exhibited the most significant
upregulation among all differentially expressed heat shock factors (Supplementary
Table 3). Based on these findings, we hypothesize that PtHSF2 is actively involved in
the regulation of the heat stress response, which is why we focused on investigating its
role in the heat stress response mechanism in this study. (L. No. 135-137)

Response: Thank you for your insightful comment.Cells used for molecular validation

clarified these growth conditions and the stage in the Methods section. (L. No. 725-727)

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
I thank the authors for having addressed my comments points by points. The additional
results and information provided are substantial. To my understanding, however, I
reckon that some of these results are not consistent with a natural role (i.e. in WT) of
PtHSF2 in P. tricornutum thermal tolerance. This is based on the following three points:
(1) Cell volume and tolerance to increased temperature – Fig.1E and 3D.
It is correct that the volume of P. tricornutum WT cell increases (by only ca. 10-20%)
in response to increased temperature (references 79 and 80 provided in the response
and this work). However, these references and the present work do not establish a causal
relationship between the increase in cell volume and the tolerance to elevated
temperature. In addition, the PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like overexpressing and knock-
down lines, as the WT line, do present such increase in cell volume in response to
increased temperature suggesting that this phenomenon, if of any role in the acclimation
to elevated temperature, is independent of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment.We fully acknowledge the
point raised. While both the literature and our current findings indicate a modest
increase in cell volume in response to elevated temperature, we recognize that this
change is not directly correlated with enhanced thermal tolerance. The observed
increase in cell volume seems to be a general physiological response of P. tricornutum
to temperature stress, rather than a specific adaptive mechanism contributing to thermal
tolerance.In light of this, we have revised the manuscript to clarify that the increase in
cell volume is a non-specific acclimation response, and we have reframed our
conclusions to avoid any direct linkage between cell volume expansion and increased
thermal tolerance. (L. No. 456-462)
In addition, we greatly appreciate the reviewer’s perspective that cell volume changes
may be independent of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like regulation. However, based on our
findings, we propose that these genes play a critical role in modulating cell volume.
Specifically, while the RNAi lines exhibit a slight increase in cell volume under high-
temperature stress, their volumes remain significantly smaller than those of the WT.
Conversely, the overexpression lines show a pronounced increase in cell volume
compared to the WT. These results are consistent with observations under non-stress
conditions (20°C), where PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like overexpression led to increased
cell volume, while knockdown resulted in reduced cell volume (Fig. 1E and Fig. 3D).
Therefore, while the increase in cell volume under high-temperature stress may indeed
represent an acclimation response, the distinct differences observed among WT,
overexpression, and knockdown lines suggest that PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like contribute
to cell volume regulation. We acknowledge the complexity of this phenomenon and
have carefully revised the manuscript to highlight that other regulatory mechanisms
may also be involved. (L. No. 216-217, 339-342, 348, 372-376, 519-534,
Supplementary Table 7; Supplementary Fig. 6E, F; Supplementary Fig. 8B;
Supplementary Fig. 9)
We hope that this clarification and the revisions made in the manuscript address the
reviewer’s concerns.
(2) Transcriptional regulation of PtHSF2 and Cdc45-like – Fig.1A and 3A.
There is no clear positive correlation in the WT line between the expression levels of
PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like and the temperature increase. Especially, the transcription
levels of PtHSF2 and Cdc45-like are lower at 30C than at 25C. This does not agree with
the observation that the PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like overexpressing lines present an
increased tolerance to 30C compared to the WT line.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed comment and provide the following
explanations to address the concerns raised:
1. Nonlinear regulation of gene transcription in response to environmental
stimuli: Environmental stimuli often induce gene expression changes that do
not necessarily exhibit a linear correlation with the intensity of the stimulus.Our
results indicate that while the transcription levels of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like
at 30°C were lower than those at 25°C, their levels at 30°C were significantly
higher than at the optimal growth temperature of 20°C (Fig. 1A and Fig. 3A).
This demonstrates a clear responsiveness of these genes to elevated
temperatures, although the relationship between transcription levels and
temperature does not follow a simple linear trend. Similar nonlinear
transcriptional responses have been widely documented in other systems. For
instance: In yeast species exposed to temperatures ranging from 10°C to 46°C,
Hsp70 expression peaked 6–8°C above the optimal growth temperature, with
expression levels declining at higher temperatures 1; In Heterosigma akashiwo,
CO₂-responsive genes, such as SLC4 (SLC4 family bicarbonate transporter),
ALAT_GGAT (alanine aminotransferase), and CA (carbonic anhydrase),
exhibited peak transcription levels at 400–600 ppm CO₂ but decreased at higher
concentrations 2; In human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells and cochlear tissues
exposed to cisplatin-induced stress, the transcription levels of stress-related
genes such as Chop (C/EBP homologous protein) and DR5 (death receptor 5)
initially rose with increasing cisplatin concentrations but decreased once a
threshold concentration was surpassed 3; Similarly, in human intervertebral disc
NP (nucleus pulposus) cells exposed to varying pH levels (7.4, 7.1, 6.8, and 6.5),
the expression of TIMP-1 (tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases 1) initially
decreased with increasing acidity (pH 7.4–7.1) but then increased as the pH
decreased further (pH 7.1–6.5) 4.
2. The dual role of HSFs in cold and heat stress responses: HSFs are well-
established mediators of abiotic stress responses 5, with individual HSFs often
responding to multiple stressors 6. For example, in wheat seedlings, TaHSF3 is
upregulated under both low and high temperatures, and its overexpression in
Arabidopsis enhances tolerance to extreme temperatures 7. Similarly, in animals,
the relative expression levels of HSF1 and HSP70 have been observed to
increase under both heat and cold stress conditions 8. In alignment with these,
our findings demonstrate that PtHSF2 was significantly upregulated at both low
(15°C) and high temperatures (25°C and 30°C) (Fig. 1A), highlighting its dual
role in mediating responses to both cold and heat stress.
3. The incomplete correlation between gene transcription levels and protein
abundance: In both bacteria and eukaryotes, intracellular protein
concentrations are generally correlated with the abundances of their
corresponding mRNAs, but the correlation is not particularly strong, with the
squared Pearson correlation coefficient (R²) typically around 0.40 9. This
suggests that a decrease in transcription levels does not necessarily result in a
proportional decrease in protein abundance. Additionally, during stress
responses, post-transcriptional and post-translational regulatory mechanisms
may play critical roles in modulating the levels and functions of mRNAs and
proteins 10. Therefore, it is insufficient to evaluate gene function based solely
on transcriptional levels. Moreover, a decline in transcription levels may
represent an energy-saving strategy under extreme conditions.
In conclusion, although the transcription levels of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like at 30°C
were lower than those at 25°C, they remained significantly elevated at both 25°C and
30°C compared to those at the optimal growth temperature (20°C). These findings
support the roles of these genes in temperature stress responses.
To address this apparent inconsistency, we further assessed the protein expression
levels of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like under different temperature conditions. As shown
in Supplementary Fig. 2F and Supplementary Fig. 7F, PtHSF2 levels in the PtHSF2-
proH1 strain, driven by the HSF2 promoter, and PtCdc45-like levels in the PtCdc45-
like-proC1 strain, driven by the Cdc45-like promoter, exhibit a clear linear increase
with rising temperatures. These results suggest that post-transcriptional or translational
regulation could contribute to the observed increased protein abundance at 30°C,
aligning with the enhanced heat tolerance observed in the overexpression lines. (L. No.
163-166, 295-298, 467-497)
(3) Thermal tolerance of siPtHSF2 and siPtCdc45-like lines – Fig.1C and 3C.
The siPtHSF2 and siPtCdc45-like lines present a tolerance to increased temperature
similar to the WT line suggesting that PtHSF2 and Cdc45-like do not play a crucial role
in thermal tolerance.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful observation regarding the thermal
tolerance of siPtHSF2 and siPtCdc45-like lines presented in Fig. 1C and Fig. 3C. The
comment that these lines exhibit a thermal tolerance similar to the WT raises important
points regarding the roles of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like in thermal stress responses.
Below, we provide a detailed response and clarification:

effectively reduced PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like transcription levels, it did not
achieve complete suppression. This incomplete silencing likely retains a level
of gene functionality sufficient to sustain the baseline thermal tolerance
observed in these lines. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2D and Supplementary
Fig. 7D, the gene expression levels of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like were reduced
by approximately 77.9% and 73.5%, respectively, leaving residual activity that
may obscure phenotypic differences under the tested conditions.
2. Potential compensatory mechanisms: Thermal tolerance is likely governed
by a network of genes and pathways with overlapping or compensatory
functions. While PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like are involved in thermal stress
responses, other heat shock factors or regulatory proteins may compensate for
their partial loss of function. Notably, P. tricornutum possesses 69 heat shock
factors (HSFs), suggesting potential redundancy or functional overlap. We
hypothesize that homologous genes may compensate for the loss of PtHSF2 in
siPtHSF2 lines, preserving thermal tolerance.

reconsidered the function of PtCdc45-like in thermal responses. Given its
established role in DNA replication during the S phase, the enhanced thermal
tolerance observed in PtCdc45-like overexpression lines may result indirectly
from its effects on DNA replication and cell cycle regulation. Our findings
reveal that PtCdc45-like overexpression induced slower cell growth (Fig. 3C)
and cell cycle arrest (Supplementary Fig. 8A) under non-stress conditions
(20°C). These findings align with previous studies indicating that Cdc45
overexpression causes severe replication stress, leading to cell cycle arrest and
proliferation inhibition 11, 12. Mechanistically, replication stress caused by
Cdc45 overexpression results in replication fork stalling and activates the
ATM/Chk2 (ataxia telangiectasia mutated/checkpoint kinase 2) signaling
pathway 11. Our findings reveal that under non-temperature stress conditions,
the overexpression of PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like markedly increased the
transcriptional levels of ATM and ATR (ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related)
levels (Supplementary Table 7; Supplementary Fig. 8B; Supplementary Fig. 9
A, B).
ATM and ATR are critical kinases that govern cell cycle and replication
checkpoints by phosphorylating the checkpoint effector kinases Chk2 and Chk1
in response to DNA damage 13. This activation initiates DNA repair mechanisms,
ensuring that damaged DNA is adequately repaired before progression into the
next cell cycle phase 13. Our results indicate that at 30°C, the transcriptional
levels of ATM and ATR were significantly elevated in both PtHSF2 and
PtCdc45-like overexpression lines (Supplementary Fig. 6E, F; Supplementary
Fig. 9C, D). This upregulation likely promotes the repair of heat-induced DNA
damage, thereby enhancing cellular heat stress responses and improving
survival under elevated temperatures.
We have revised the Discussion section to address this comment and provide further
clarification. We hope this explanation comprehensively addresses the reviewer’s
concerns. (L. No. 519-546)
It is a consequent and important work, but as it stands, I think that the results are not
supporting and congruent enough for the manuscript to be published in Nature
Communications.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Diatoms are a crucial component of marine ecosystems, recognized for their broad environmental adaptability and wide temperature tolerance. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying their adaptability to diverse temperatures are unknown. In this study, we discover that heat shock transcription factors (HSFs) are potentially important for thermal tolerance in diatoms. Our study focuses on PtHSF2, annotated as HSF2 in Phaeodactylum tricornutum’s genome, which is ubiquitous in diatoms. Overexpression of PtHSF2 markedly enhances thermal tolerance and increases cell size; causes significant differential expression of several genes, including cell division cycle protein 45-like (PtCdc45-like), ATM (ataxia telangiectasia mutated), ATR (ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related), light-harvesting complex protein 2 (Lhcx2), and fatty acid desaturase. Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag) and CUT&Tag-qPCR analyses demonstrate that PtHSF2 directly targets and upregulates PtCdc45-like and Lhcx2 while downregulating ATP-binding cassette transporter. Functional validation of PtCdc45-like shows that its overexpression results in larger cell size, enhances antioxidant capacity, and improves cell survival at elevated temperatures. Collectively, our findings elucidate the molecular mechanism by which PtHSF2 mediates high-temperature tolerance in diatoms and validate the functions of its target gene PtCdc45-like. These results highlight the importance of HSFs in diatom temperature adaptation and provide insights into temperature acclimation in microalgae.

---

## Introduction

Global warming, primarily driven by the greenhouse effect, has led to the oceans sequestering over 90% of the excess heat on Earth since 19701. The oceans play a pivotal role in maintaining the planet’s thermal balance, yet the rise in sea temperatures has had detrimental impacts on marine ecosystems. These impacts include substantial coral reef degradation2, declines in marine fauna populations3, and reductions in marine biodiversity4. Marine phytoplankton, critical to oceanic ecosystems, contribute nearly half of global primary productivity5 and are essential in regulating Earth’s climate. Notably, among various phytoplankton groups such as diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria, and coccolithophores, diatoms are distinguished by their extensive temperature tolerance6, highlighting their pivotal role in responding to climate change.

Diatoms, which are vital to Earth’s ecosystems and account for approximately one-fifth of global carbon dioxide fixation annually7, are at the forefront of research in the context of global warming. The warming trend has been linked to potential reductions in diatom abundance worldwide by at least 10%, due to increased ocean stratification8. However, there are perspectives suggesting that this stratification may boost diatom productivity and organic carbon output9. A groundbreaking study combining genomic and phenotypic analyses reveals rapid evolutionary adaptation of diatoms to higher temperatures10, underscoring their crucial role as marine phytoplankton in adapting to climate change. Therefore, investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying diatom thermal tolerance is not only of scientific importance but also key to foreseeing and understanding shifts in future marine ecosystems.

Heat shock transcription factors (HSFs) are highly conserved DNA-binding proteins in eukaryotes, playing a crucial role in environmental adaptation by finely tuning gene transcription and enhancing stress resistance11–13. Phaeodactylum tricornutum, a model diatom species widely distributed in coastal and inland waters, exhibits remarkable cell plasticity, including size variation and morphological changes among oval, fusiform, and triradiate forms14. This unique plasticity, combined with its exceptional environmental adaptability, enables P. tricornutum to thrive in highly unstable conditions, such as estuaries and rock pools14. Notably, P. tricornutum exhibits significant temperature adaptability15,16, surviving in natural environments from the tropics to subarctic regions17, and growing in laboratory conditions from 5 to 28°C18,19. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its thermotolerance remain enigmatic.

The effects of temperature on diatom growth and physiology are well-studied20–22. High-throughput sequencing technologies have paved the way for investigating the molecular mechanisms of diatom responses to temperature stress. Many studies have explored these mechanisms using genomics10, transcriptomics23–25, and proteomics26, providing valuable insights into diatom thermal tolerance. However, these studies primarily focus on omics data, with limited functional analyses of key temperature-responsive genes, especially HSFs. In this study, we investigated the functional mechanism of a conserved diatom HSF in P. tricornutum, which may offer new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying thermal tolerance in diatoms.

---

## Results

Diatoms, widely distributed in marine ecosystems, are ubiquitous in nearly all aquatic habitats28. Different diatom species exhibit distinct thermal tolerance ranges. For instance, Chaetoceros tenuissimus grows optimally between 25 to 30°C29, while Fragilariopsis cylindrus thrives at −1 to 10°C30. T. pseudonana, Fistulifera solaris, and P. tricornutum have thermal tolerance ranges of 10–35°C10,31, 15–35°C32,33, and 5–28°C18,19, respectively. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying the thermal adaptability of diatoms, an analysis of transcription factor abundance and proportion was conducted in 15 diatom species with sequenced genomes. Results revealed that HSFs are the most abundant transcription factors family in diatoms, ranging from tens to hundreds of genes (Supplementary Table 1). For example, T. weissflogii harbors 393 HSF-encoding genes, constituting 53% of its total transcription factors, while dinoflagellates, coccolithophores, and green algae possess fewer than 10 HSFs, accounting for only 0–7.2% of their transcription factors. Given the global distribution and extensive temperature adaptability of diatoms, it was hypothesized that HSFs play a crucial role in their environmental adaptation. Consistent with previous reports27, we found that P. tricornutum possessed 69 HSF genes, representing the highest proportion (44.2%) among all transcription factors. An analysis of transcriptome data from the MMETSP project34 and the re-assembly data by Johnson et al.35 indicated that 38 HSF genes are actively expressed in P. tricornutum (Supplementary Data 1). Additionally, we observed the expression of HSF orthologues in other species (Supplementary Data 1). We speculate that these HSFs may play significant regulatory roles under specific stress conditions, including high temperature, light stress, and other environmental stresses.

Phylogenetic analysis categorized the 69 HSFs into four major groups: Group I, Group II, Group III, and Group IV (Supplementary Fig. 1A). Except for Group II, the other groups were further subdivided into multiple subclasses. Group IV HSFs displayed closer homology with HSFs from Emiliania huxleyi. Overall, P. tricornutum HSFs were more closely related to each other than to HSFs from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii or Arabidopsis thaliana. Notably, PtHSF2 (Phatr3_J55070) showed the most significant upregulation among the differentially expressed HSFs under elevated temperature conditions (Supplementary Data 2), with its transcript levels varying significantly with temperature changes (15°C to 30°C), peaking at 25°C, followed by 15°C, 30°C, and 20°C (Fig. 1A), suggesting that PtHSF2 may play a crucial role in temperature response.

Furthermore, the analysis of the taxonomic distribution of PtHSF2 homologs in the ocean revealed that 99% of the hits in the marine EUK-SMAGs (Eukaryotes Single-Cell and Metagenome Assembled Genomes) database were from diatoms (Bacillariophyta) (Supplementary Fig. 1B), indicating that diatoms are the primary hosts of this gene. This finding suggests that PtHSF2 is widely present in diatoms and may play a crucial role in their biological functions or adaptation mechanisms. Supplementary Fig. 1C shows that the abundance of PtHSF2 homologs is highest at higher latitudes and relatively low in tropical regions, which could be attributed to differing environmental conditions and ecological niches in these areas. Although diatoms exhibit broad temperature tolerance, they generally thrive better in cooler waters36.

SMART (Simple Modular Architecture Research Tool) domain annotation identified a conserved HSF domain in PtHSF2 between amino acids 89 and 188 (Supplementary Fig. 2A). Annotated as HSF2 in the P. tricornutum genome, it was named PtHSF2. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that genes with higher homology to PtHSF2 were derived from other diatom species, such as F. solaris, Pseudo-nitzschia multistriata, and T. pseudonana (Supplementary Fig. 2B). To assess PtHSF2’ regulatory function in microalgae, overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi) plasmids were separately constructed (Fig. 1B). Through genomic polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (Supplementary Fig. 2C), quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) (Supplementary Fig. 2D), and western blotting (Supplementary Fig. 2E), three overexpression lines (PtHSF2-1, PtHSF2-2, and PtHSF2-3) and three silenced lines (siPtHSF2-1, siPtHSF2-2, and siPtHSF2-3) were successfully established. We measured PtHSF2 protein levels in the PtHSF2 overexpression strain (PtHSF2-proH1) at four temperatures (15°C, 20°C, 25°C, and 30°C) and found a significant increase at elevated temperatures (25°C and 30°C) (Supplementary Fig. 2F).

Alignment analysis of the coding regions of the remaining 68 HSF genes from P. tricornutum with dsPtHSF2 revealed that only 8 HSF genes, including Phatr3_J38294, Phatr3_J48667, Phatr3_J48572, Phatr3_J42824, Phatr3_J45391, Phatr3_EG02624, Phatr3_J50136, and Phatr3_EG00212, contained perfectly matching segments with dsPtHSF2, all of which were shorter than 16bp (Supplementary Fig. 3A). According to Chen et al.37, such short matches are insufficient to cause off-target effects. Furthermore, analysis of the relative transcription levels of these 8 HSF genes showed no significant downregulation (Supplementary Fig. 3B). These results indicate that RNAi targeting PtHSF2 did not cause off-target effects among its paralogues.

To characterize the thermal tolerance of PtHSF2-transformed microalgae, cells were cultured separately at 15°C, 20°C, 25°C, and 30°C. Cell density monitoring revealed that PtHSF2 overexpression cell lines exhibited lower growth rates at 15°C, 20°C, and 25°C compared to WT cells and the RNAi lines (Fig. 1C). While temperatures above 25°C impaired growth, and 30°C exposure for over three days severely inhibited it, PtHSF2 overexpression lines had significantly higher cell density than WT cells at 30°C (Fig. 1C). Confocal microscopy and Nile red staining revealed increased cell size and neutral lipid content in overexpression lines, particularly at 30°C (Fig. 1D–F). Additionally, lipid droplets were observed outside of the PtHSF2-1 cells under 30°C, potentially due to cell rupture or active secretion (Fig. 1D). Previous studies have demonstrated that microalgae actively secrete lipid droplets during periods of high lipid synthesis38. Quantitative analysis showed that cell volume in overexpression lines was 2.1–2.4 times larger than WT cells at 30°C, while knockdown lines were significantly smaller (Fig. 1E).

Thermal stress often impairs photosystem II (PSII), leading to reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and lipid peroxidation39,40. Therefore, ROS and lipid peroxides, such as malondialdehyde (MDA), an abundant byproduct of lipid peroxidation41, serve as indicators of oxidative stress. Analysis of cell survival rates demonstrated that PtHSF2 overexpressing lines exhibited significantly higher survival rates at 30°C compared to WT cells (Fig. 1G). Moreover, overexpression lines exhibited significantly lower ROS (Fig. 1H) and MDA levels (Supplementary Fig. 4A) and higher antioxidant enzyme activities, including superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT) (Supplementary Fig. 4B, C). The lipid saturation index was significantly lower in the overexpressing lines and higher in the RNAi lines compared to the WT (Supplementary Fig. 4D). These results suggest that PtHSF2 may mediate the cell’s thermal response by regulating the expression of genes related to cell size, lipid synthesis, and antioxidant defense.

We employed RNA-seq, CUT&Tag, and CUT&Tag-qPCR techniques to unravel the functional mechanisms governed by PtHSF2. The number and quality of sequencing reads from RNA-seq and CUT&Tag libraries were presented in the Supplementary Data 3 and 4, highlighting the sequencing depth and overal data quality across all samples. RNA-seq analysis revealed 1912 significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the PtHSF2-1 versus WT comparison, with 940 upregulated and 972 downregulated. In the PtHSF2-2 versus WT comparison, 2,404 DEGs were identified, including 1,121 upregulated and 1,283 downregulated. Among these, 1449 DEGs were shared between the two PtHSF2 overexpressing lines, comprising 676 upregulated and 773 downregulated (Supplementary Data 5). Notably, genes encoding Cdc45-like (Phatr3_J9344), light-harvesting complex protein 2 (Lhcx2, Phatr3_EG02404), fatty acid desaturase (FAD, Phatr3_J46275), as well as ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM, Phatr3_J51040) and ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related (ATR, Phatr3_J44708), were significantly upregulated, while an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter (Phatr3_J42881) containing two ABC_ATPase domains, which shares high homology with F. solaris and Cylindrotheca closterium, was significantly downregulated (Supplementary Data 6–8 and Supplementary Fig. 5A, B). Additionally, the expression levels of 12 PtHSF2 homologs exhibited significant changes, with 5 genes upregulated and 7 downregulated (Supplementary Data 8).

Gene Ontology (GO) annotation and enrichment analysis of the 1449 DEGs revealed that 30.9% participated in cellular processes under the “biological process” category, with 15.0% upregulated and 15.9% downregulated (Fig. 2A and Supplementary Data 9). In the “molecular function” category, 29.4% of DEGs were associated with catalytic activity, with 12.6% upregulated and 16.8% downregulated (Fig. 2B). For the “cellular component” category, DEGs enriched in “cell” and “cell part” terms both accounted for 36.7%, comprising 16.9% upregulated and 19.8% downregulated genes (Fig. 2C). KEGG pathway analysis unveiled significant enrichment of genes involved in cell cycle regulation, antioxidant defense, fatty acids synthesis, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling, and carbohydrate metabolism (Supplementary Data 6). Among these, two mitochondrial inner membrane proteins, MPV17 (Phatr3_J15341 and Phatr3_Jdraft223), associated with antioxidant processes42, were significantly upregulated (Supplementary Data 6). Collectively, these results highlight that PtHSF2 overexpression profoundly influences genes linked to cell cycle regulation and environmental information processing.

CUT&Tag, a potent method for investigating transcription factor-DNA interactions43, identified 295 potential PtHSF2 target genes (Supplementary Data 10), which underwent GO annotation analysis (Fig. 2D–F). These target genes were enriched in catalytic (22.4%) and binding activities (31.2%), participating in intracellular biological processes (32.9%) (Fig. 2D, E). Moreover, a substantial proportion was associated with membrane components (19.3%) and cellular components (38.3%) (Fig. 2F and Supplementary Data 10), suggesting PtHSF2’s involvement in regulating cellular structures and membrane composition.

CUT&Tag, a potent method for investigating transcription factor-DNA interactions43, identified 295 potential PtHSF2 target genes (Supplementary Data 10), which underwent GO annotation analysis (Fig. 2D–F). These target genes were enriched in catalytic (22.4%) and binding activities (31.2%), participating in intracellular biological processes (32.9%) (Fig. 2D, E). Moreover, a substantial proportion was associated with membrane components (19.3%) and cellular components (38.3%) (Fig. 2F and Supplementary Data 10), suggesting PtHSF2’s involvement in regulating cellular structures and membrane composition.

CUT&Tag and CUT&Tag-qPCR analyses were performed. The Venn diagram (Fig. 2G) revealed 35 intersecting genes between potential targets and DEGs (Supplementary Data 11), comprising 18 upregulated and 17 downregulated genes, including Cdc45-like (Phatr3_J9344), Lhcx2 (Phatr3_EG02404), and the ABC transporter (Phatr3_J42881). The limited overlap between DEGs and potential targets likely stems from several factors. First, TFs can regulate gene expression both directly and indirectly44, with some targets showing no detectable expression changes45–47. Second, while RNA-seq offers broad coverage, it lacks specificity, whereas CUT&Tag provides high specificity by targeting proteins of interest with specific antibodies43. Signal intensity analysis around transcription start sites (TSS) showed a significant enrichment peak at 8.25 for PtHSF2, indicating its primary binding sites at the TSS regions, which were absent in IgG controls (Fig. 2H). Using the MEME algorithm48, we identified the top three DNA-binding motifs for PtHSF2 (Fig. 2I), with the most prominent motif being the sequence “GGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAG.” This sequence represents a putative consensus motif, indicating a conserved recognition pattern across genomic sites. CUT&Tag-qPCR further confirmed PtHSF2’s binding to promoter regions of Cdc45-like (Phatr3_J9344), Lhcx2 (Phatr3_EG02404), and ABC (Phatr3_J42881) transporter genes in both overexpressing lines (Fig. 2J–L).

TF scan positively or negatively regulate the transcription of target genes38,44,49. To elucidate how PtHSF2 modulates its targets, we analyzed transcription levels of potential target genes. In PtHSF2-overexpressing cells, Cdc45-like and Lhcx2 were significantly upregulated, while the ABC transporter was notably downregulated (Fig. 2M–O). The upregulation of FAD (Phatr3_J46275) in overexpressing lines and its downregulation in RNAi lines (Fig. 2P and Supplementary Data 6) corresponded with changes in unsaturated fatty acid content (Supplementary Fig. 4D). However, CUT&Tag did not detect direct targeting of the FAD promoter, suggesting that PtHSF2 regulates FAD indirectly. Interestingly, the regulatory trends for target genes at 30°C (Supplementary Fig. 6A-F) were consistent with those observed at 20°C (Fig. 2M–P; Supplementary Data 5), suggesting that PtHSF2’s regulatory mechanisms remain stable across these temperature conditions.

In the WT background, PtCdc45-like transcription increased from 15°C to 25°C but declined at 30°C compared to 25°C (Fig. 3A), suggesting its critical role in high-temperature responses. To elucidate PtCdc45-like’s biological function, we employed bioinformatics and molecular biology approaches. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that PtCdc45-like coding region spans 2274 bp, encoding a conserved Cdc45-like protein domain between amino acids 29 and 754 (Supplementary Fig. 7A). Phylogenetic analysis showed that PtCdc45-like is evolutionarily conserved among diatoms (Supplementary Fig. 7B).

To characterize its function, overexpression and RNAi plasmids were constructed (Fig. 3B). Putative positive transformants were selected based on bleomycin resistance and validated through genomic PCR, qPCR, and western blot analyses, resulting in six confirmed lines: three overexpression lines (PtCdc45-like-1, −2, −3) and three RNAi lines (siPtCdc45-like-1, −2, −3) (Supplementary Fig. 7C–E). qPCR analysis revealed transcription levels of PtCdc45-like were 2.6-to 3.8-fold higher in the overexpression lines and reduced to 20.2–29.3% of WT levels in RNAi lines (Supplementary Fig. 7D). Western blotting confirmed specific protein expression (~86.9 kDa) in transformants but not in WT cells (Supplementary Fig. 7E). Protein level analysis across varying temperatures demonstrated a temperature-dependent increase in PtCdc45-like protein levels in the PtCdc45-like-proC1 overexpression strain (Supplementary Fig. 7F).

Overexpressing lines exhibited significantly reduced cell densities compared to WT and RNAi lines at 15–25°C, but notably higher densities at 30°C (Fig. 3C). Under normal growth conditions (20°C), overexpression lines displayed significantly larger cell volumes than WT, while RNAi lines had smaller cells, with cell size increasing further at higher temperatures (Fig. 3D, E). These results highlight PtCdc45-like as a key regulator of cell size in P. tricornutum. Notably, the total dry weight of cell pellets, normalized by cell number, revealed that larger cell volumes correlated with higher average cell dry weight (Fig. 3F).

Cell plasticity is influenced by membrane fluidity and cell wall flexibility. The fusiform structure of P. tricornutum, lacking a silicified cell wall50, may facilitate cell size plasticity. Consistent with this, overexpression lines exhibited a lower lipid saturation index, while RNAi lines had higher indices (Fig. 3G). This suggests a positive correlation between cell size and the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids, supported by the upregulation of FAD (Phatr3_J46275) in overexpression lines and its downregulation in RNAi lines (Supplementary Fig. 7G). These findings align with those observed in PtHSF2 transgenic lines (Fig. 2P) and prior studies linking desaturase activity to unsaturated fatty acid synthesis51,52. In microalgae, fatty acids primarily exist as triacylglycerols (TAGs), phospholipids, and glycolipids, with phospholipids and glycolipids serving as the primary components of membranes53. Accordingly, we hypothesize that larger cells had a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their cell membranes, contributing to enhanced membrane fluidity.

Overexpression lines exhibited lower maximum quantum yield of photosystem II (Fv/Fm) than WT, while RNAi lines showed no difference (Fig. 3H). Interestingly, Lhcx2 (Phatr3_EG02404) transcription decreased in overexpression lines but increased in RNAi lines (Supplementary Fig. 7H), contrasting with its regulation in PtHSF2-transformed lines (Fig. 2N).

Overexpression of both PtCdc45-like and PtHSF2 resulted in comparable phenotypic changes, including increased cell size and altered lipid composition. Furthermore, the ABC transporter (Phatr3_J42881) was significantly downregulated in both PtCdc45-like and PtHSF2 overexpressing lines and upregulated in the RNAi lines (Fig. 2O and Supplementary Fig. 7I). This transporter’s ABC_ATPase domain (Supplementary Fig. 5A), associated with mitochondrial mRNA processing54, suggests that its downregulation may impair mitochondrial function, contributing to slower growth.

Cell cycle progression analysis revealed that overexpression lines (PtHSF2-1 and PtCdc45-like-1) had higher proportions of cells in the S and G2 phases, indicating accumulation or arrest, whereas RNAi lines displayed distributions similar to WT cells (Supplementary Fig. 8A). This is consistent with differential expression of cell cycle-related genes in overexpression lines (Supplementary Data 6; Supplementary Fig. 6E, F; Supplementary Fig. 8B; Supplementary Fig. 9), which may contribute to the observed cell accumulation or arrest during these phases. Among these genes, the key kinases regulating cell cycle and replication checkpoints, ATM and ATR55, were significantly upregulated, suggesting the activation of cell cycle checkpoints. In addition to these cell cycle-related genes, PtCdc45-like significantly altered the transcription levels of FAD, Lhcx2, and ABC (Supplementary Fig. 7G–I). Specifically, its effects on FAD and ABC were consistent with those of PtHSF2, whereas its effect on Lhcx2 was opposite.

To investigate the regulatory relationship between PtCdc45-like and the transcriptional variability of FAD, Lhcx2, ABC, ATM, and ATR we first examined PtHSF2 transcription in PtCdc45-like overexpression and RNAi lines. The results revealed that PtHSF2 was upregulated in the overexpression lines and downregulated in the RNAi lines (Fig. 4A). Combined with our earlier observation that PtHSF2 activates PtCdc45-like transcription, this finding suggests the existence of a positive feedback loop between PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like.

To further elucidate the regulatory interactions, two types of transgenic cell lines were constructed: Ho-Ci (PtHSF2 overexpression combined with PtCdc45-like knockdown) and Hi-Co (PtHSF2 knockdown combined with PtCdc45-like overexpression). Six lines—Ho-Ci-1, Ho-Ci-2, Ho-Ci-3, Hi-Co-1, Hi-Co-2, and Hi-Co-3—were successfully validated (Supplementary Fig. 10A–F). Next, we assessed FAD and ABC transcription levels in these cell lines. The results indicated that knocking down PtCdc45-like in the PtHSF2 overexpression background did not affect FAD and ABC, and similarly, overexpressing PtCdc45-like in the PtHSF2 knockdown background had no impact on these genes (Fig. 4B, C). These findings suggest that the regulation of FAD and ABC is predominantly mediated by PtHSF2, with the influence of PtCdc45-like being exerted indirectly through its positive feedback on PtHSF2.

In contrast, Lhcx2 transcription was significantly altered in both Ho-Ci and Hi-Co lines, as knocking down PtCdc45-like in the PtHSF2 overexpression background increased Lhcx2 while overexpressing PtCdc45-like in the PtHSF2 knockdown background decreased Lhcx2 (Fig. 4D), indicating that Lhcx2 transcription is influenced by PtCdc45-like. Combined with the data from Fig. 2K, N, these results suggest that Lhcx2 is co-regulated by PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like, with PtCdc45-like acting as a repressor. Whether this repression is direct or indirect remains to be investigated. ATM and ATR were markedly downregulated in the Ho-Ci lines but upregulated in the Hi-Co lines (Fig. 4E, F). Moreover, both genes were significantly upregulated in PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like overexpression lines (Supplementary Data 6; Supplementary Fig. 6E, F; Supplementary Fig. 8B; Supplementary Fig. 9), suggesting that PtHSF2 may regulate these genes via PtCdc45-like.

Under normal growth conditions (20°C), knocking down PtCdc45-like in the PtHSF2 overexpression background alleviated the growth retardation (Fig. 4G) and cell enlargement (Fig. 4H) caused by PtHSF2 overexpression. However, under heat stress (30°C), PtCdc45-like knockdown significantly reduced cell density (Fig. 4G). Conversely, overexpressing PtCdc45-like in the PtHSF2 knockdown background yielded the opposite results (Fig. 4G, H). These findings highlight PtCdc45-like as a critical mediator of PtHSF2-regulated cell size and thermal response. Overall, PtHSF2 positively regulates PtCdc45-like and Lhcx2 while negatively regulating ABC and indirectly regulating FAD, with a positive feedback loop between PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like, and PtCdc45-like acting as a repressor of Lhcx2.

The optimum growth temperature for P. tricornutum (CCMP2561) under laboratory conditions was 20°C. Elevated temperatures negatively impacted cellular growth, often leading to growth inhibition or cell death. Fig. 5A demonstrates that the inhibition rates at 25°C and 30°C were significantly higher in WT cells compared to PtCdc45-like overexpressing cells. Notably, PtCdc45-like overexpressing cells did not show a growth advantage at lower temperatures (15°C and 20°C) (Fig. 3C), suggesting that PtCdc45-like overexpression enhances heat tolerance rather than cold tolerance. To further investigate the thermal tolerance conferred by PtCdc45-like overexpression, we assessed cell survival rates and redox levels under high-temperature conditions (25°C and 30°C). Given the clear growth trend observed at 25°C (Fig. 3C), survival rate analysis was not performed at this temperature. After 13 days of incubation at 30°C, the survival rate of WT cells was only 23.6%, whereas PtCdc45-like overexpression lines (PtCdc45-like-1, PtCdc45-like-2, and PtCdc45-like-3) exhibited significantly higher survival rates of 76.7, 72.5, and 65.0%, respectively (Fig. 5B).

Furthermore, ROS (Fig. 5C) and MDA (Fig. 5D) levels were markedly lower in PtCdc45-like overexpressing cells compared to WT cells, indicating a diminished sensitivity to high-temperature stress. Since oxygenic photosynthesis is a major source of ROS production56, the relatively lower ROS levels observed in PtCdc45-like overexpressing cells could be attributed to the significant suppression of Fv/Fm (Fig. 3H) and the downregulation of Lhcx2 transcription (Supplementary Fig. 7H). Despite no significant increase in SOD levels in overexpressing cells at 30°C compared to WT cells (Fig. 5E), CAT levels were markedly higher in the overexpressing cells (Fig. 5F). Conversely, the PtCdc45-like RNAi lines showed no significant differences in antioxidant enzyme levels compared to WT (Fig. 5D–F). Collectively, these data provided compelling evidence that PtCdc45-like overexpression augmented cellular antioxidant defenses, thereby improving cell tolerance to elevated temperatures.

Both PtHSF2 and PtCdc45-like were identified as crucial contributors to heat tolerance in P. tricornutum. However, it remains unclear whether this mechanism is conserved across other diatom species. To investigate, we subjected T. weissflogii to 20°C, 30°C, and 35°C, followed by transcriptome analysis (quality control details in Supplementary Data 12). Compared to 20°C, the PtHSF2 orthologue in T. weissflogii (snap_masked-ctg119-processed-gene-4.14-mRNA-1, 48.5% similarity) was upregulated 1.21-fold at 30°C and 1.92-fold at 35°C, with the PtCdc45-like orthologue (snap_masked-ctg1929-processed-gene-0.66-mRNA-1, 53.4% similarity) also exhibiting an upregulation trend (Supplementary Data 13). These results suggest that HSF2 may serve as a key regulator of heat tolerance in diatoms and that this regulatory mechanism may be broadly conserved across diatom species.
